common_name: Ice Crystal Oakleaf Hydrangea (Dissected-Leaf Compact Oakleaf Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Ice Crystal (sold under this trade name) stays notably compact, so it fits foundation beds and large containers where a standard oakleaf hydrangea would outgrow the space.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade, avoiding hot afternoon sun that can scorch the finely cut foliage. Ice Crystal is distinguished among oakleaf hydrangeas by its heavily dissected, almost fern-like lobed leaves, which give the shrub a lacy texture through the growing season before shifting to silvery-purple tones in fall. It carries the same upright cream-white conical flower panicles as the species, but on a much more compact, rounded frame that suits smaller gardens. Because it blooms on old wood, prune only immediately after flowering to avoid removing next year's buds.

common_name: Alison Oakleaf Hydrangea (Broad Spreading Giant Oakleaf Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and allow generous room — Alison eventually spreads as wide as, or wider than, it grows tall.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, giving Alison plenty of horizontal room to develop its wide, arching branch structure. Selected as a sister seedling to the popular 'Alice' cultivar, Alison grows into one of the largest oakleaf hydrangeas available, eventually reaching roughly 8 to 10 feet tall and equally wide, with upright creamy-white flower panicles held above the foliage in early summer. The deeply lobed leaves turn rich burgundy and bronze in fall and persist for weeks, and the exfoliating cinnamon bark provides winter structure once they drop. Because flower buds form on old wood, limit pruning to right after bloom and only to remove dead or crossing branches.

common_name: Bounty Smooth Hydrangea (Sturdy-Stemmed Mophead Smooth Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to partial sun; Bounty's sturdier stems hold up its mophead blooms better than older smooth hydrangea selections.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to partial sun; Bounty offers the same billowing white mophead display as 'Annabelle' and 'Grandiflora' but on notably sturdier, more upright stems that resist flopping after rain. Its individual flower heads are somewhat smaller and its foliage larger than the classic selections, giving the multi-layered blooms a distinctive, cloud-like texture from early to late summer. Like other smooth hydrangeas, it flowers on new wood, so it tolerates a hard cutback to 6-12 inches in late winter and will still bloom reliably that same season. This native selection adapts to a wide range of soils and is among the most cold-hardy hydrangeas available.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center Wild Hydrangea Trial

common_name: Candybelle Bubblegum Hydrangea (Compact Bubblegum-Pink Smooth Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Candybelle Bubblegum (sold under this trade name) stays compact enough for foundation plantings and mixed borders.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun. Candybelle Bubblegum was bred from a cross using 'Annabelle' as the pollen parent and produces domed flower heads in a saturated bubblegum pink, a striking departure from the white blooms typical of the species, set against foliage with a subtle bronze cast. Its thick, upright stems hold the flower heads well even after heavy rain, and like other smooth hydrangeas it blooms on new wood, so it can be cut back hard in late winter without losing the coming season's flowers. The compact, rounded habit makes it a good fit for smaller gardens where full-size smooth hydrangea cultivars would be too large.

common_name: Green Dragon Smooth Hydrangea (Dissected-Leaf Lacecap Smooth Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial sun to shade; the ragged, deeply cut foliage of Green Dragon (sold under the trade name Riven Lace) provides season-long texture even between bloom cycles.

directions: Plant in average, moist, well-drained soil in partial sun to partial shade; Green Dragon is grown chiefly for its unusual dark green foliage, which is cut so deeply and irregularly that it looks torn or fringed, giving the whole shrub a textured, almost fern-like presence long before the flowers appear. In summer it produces white lacecap flower heads, 6 to 8 inches across, with a ring of showy sterile florets surrounding the smaller fertile center flowers. It flowers on new wood, so an annual hard prune to the ground in late winter keeps the habit dense and tidy at a manageable 4 to 5 feet. Its cutting-garden and dried-arrangement value comes as much from the striking foliage as from the blooms.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center Wild Hydrangea Trial

common_name: Invincibelle Limetta Hydrangea (Lime-Green Reblooming Smooth Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Limetta's compact size and season-long color shift make it well suited to fresh and dried cut-flower use.

directions: Plant in average, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Invincibelle Limetta opens rounded flower spheres in a fresh lime green, softens to a pale green-white as they mature, and finally settles into jade green through fall, giving one plant several distinct color phases across the season. Strong, upright stems keep the flower heads from flopping even in wind and rain, and because it blooms on new growth it can be cut back hard in late winter without sacrificing the following season's display. Its compact, rounded habit fits small borders and mass plantings where full-size smooth hydrangeas would be too large.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center Wild Hydrangea Trial

common_name: Candybelle Marshmallow Hydrangea (Compact Salmon-Pink Smooth Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Candybelle Marshmallow's dense, compact frame suits small borders and mixed containers.

directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Candybelle Marshmallow forms a dense, rounded, compact shrub topped from midsummer into early fall with large umbels of light salmon-pink flowers set against toothed, dark green leaves. Its very sturdy branching habit keeps the flower heads upright without staking, distinguishing it from older, floppier smooth hydrangea types. It blooms on new wood, so a hard prune in late winter renews the plant's shape without reducing flowering, and its compact size makes it a good option where space is limited.

common_name: Mary Nell Smooth Hydrangea (Double-Ring Lacecap Smooth Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Mary Nell performs best with more shade than most smooth hydrangea cultivars, holding its foliage and flowers longer.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Mary Nell is a rare lacecap-type selection of native smooth hydrangea, originally found in the Illinois garden of the same plant breeder who introduced 'Annabelle,' and it stands out for an unusual double ring of large, showy sterile flowers encircling the smaller fertile blooms at the center. It performs best sited in shade, where it retains attractive foliage and flowers for nearly the whole growing season and draws significant pollinator activity. Like other smooth hydrangeas it blooms on new wood, so it tolerates a hard late-winter cutback and still flowers reliably that year.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center Wild Hydrangea Trial

common_name: Invincibelle Spirit II Hydrangea (Improved Pink Reblooming Smooth Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Invincibelle Spirit II improves on the original Invincibelle Spirit with sturdier stems and deeper flower color.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Invincibelle Spirit II was bred from a pink-flowered native smooth hydrangea found wild in the Blue Ridge Mountains and improves on the original Invincibelle Spirit with sturdier stems and richer color: large mophead blooms open a deep, saturated pink and gradually age to an attractive green through summer and fall. It flowers reliably on new wood, so it can be cut back hard in late winter and still put on a full display the same season, and it rebounds quickly from winter dieback in colder zones. As a native species selection it adapts to a wide range of soils and makes a good pollinator plant for borders and mass plantings.

common_name: Invincibelle Sublime Hydrangea (Lime-Green Mophead Smooth Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Invincibelle Sublime's dark foliage makes its lime-green blooms especially striking.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Invincibelle Sublime produces oversized, cloud-like mophead flower clusters in a soft lime green that contrast strikingly against unusually dark, lush green foliage, a departure from the typical white or pink smooth hydrangea palette. Sturdy stems hold the large flower heads upright through summer storms, and the blooms hold their color well when cut fresh or dried for arrangements. Because it flowers on new wood, prune it back hard in late winter to keep the plant compact and encourage a full flush of the following season's blooms.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center Wild Hydrangea Trial

common_name: FlowerFull Smooth Hydrangea (Heavy-Blooming Disease-Resistant Smooth Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; FlowerFull was bred specifically for stronger stems and cleaner foliage than older smooth hydrangea selections.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. FlowerFull is a recent breeding advance in native smooth hydrangea, selected for exceptionally sturdy stems that hold its rounded white flower heads upright through wind and rain without the flopping common to older cultivars, plus two to three times more blooms per plant across the season. Its foliage also shows notably better resistance to leaf diseases such as powdery mildew, staying clean and attractive well into late summer. Like other smooth hydrangeas it blooms on new wood, so it can be cut back hard in late winter and will still flower prolifically the same year.
